content: When administering 9% sodium chloride (NaCl) for dilution, particularly during the replacement of large volumes of albumin, it is critical to monitor and manage coagulation and hematocrit levels. Albumin has a colloid osmotic effect approximately four times greater than that of human blood. Therefore, when concentrated albumin is administered, it is essential to maintain proper hydration in the patient. Albumin is a blood-derived product, and while the risk of transmitting viral diseases or variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) is extremely low, it cannot be entirely ruled out. There is no available human or animal data to confirm or deny the presence of drug-associated risks. It is also unknown whether albumin is excreted in human breast milk. The use of 9% NaCl may be combined with saline or carbohydrate solutions through the same administration set. However, it should not be used with ethanol or protein hydrolysates, as this may result in precipitation. The product should be stored at temperatures below 30°C (86°F) and should not be frozen. To protect the solution from light, the vial should be kept in its outer carton. Do not use the solution if it appears turbid or contains deposits. Once the vial is opened, the solution must be used within four hours, and any unused portion should be discarded. In the event of an overdose, if the individual exhibits severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, emergency services (911) should be contacted immediately. Otherwise, a poison control center should be contacted right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222 for assistance. Medications should not be flushed down the toilet or poured into drains unless specifically instructed to do so. Expired or unused products should be properly discarded.
